newsitem.title: UK: Royal Shakespeare Co broadens arts sponsorship.
newsitem.headline: Royal Shakespeare Co broadens arts sponsorship.

text.p: Britain's Royal Shakespeare Co, the world's largest theatre company, is expanding arts sponsorship to embrace marketing values -- but theatre-goers may rest assured they won't be seeing corporate logos on Hamlet's costume.

Sponsorship, once a poor cousin to advertising, has become increasingly important to companies in recent years as they seek to raise brand awareness and develop closer relationships with consumers. But while sponsorship of sports teams and events has become a high-priced, high-profile business, arts sponsorship has hovered in the wings.
The Royal Shakespeare Co (RSC), however, is changing the scope of arts sponsorship deals -- and insists the change is entirely compatible with the high-brow world of Shakespearean theatre.
"We've changed the way we deal with sponsorship over the last few years," Ian Rowley, head of press and public relations for the RSC, told Reuters in an interview.

Although the RSC, like other arts organisations, had had corporate sponsors for many years, those deals were narrowly focused, Robert Fleming, the RSC's sponsorship development manager, said in an interview at the company's London home at the Barbican Theatre.
Previously, in exchange for sponsorship, companies typically received advertising space in play programmes and free tickets to productions that could be used to entertain clients.
The change in arts sponsorship in Britain traces to the 1980s, when there was much more of a directive from the government for companies to get more involved in the arts, said Fleming.

"Sponsorship grew at the RSC at a rate that was much faster than at other companies," Fleming said, because the RSC realised that good sponsorship deals were built on developing an ongoing relationship with the sponsor rather than just accepting money.

Ongoing relationships with sponsors mean showing how overseas tours of the RSC and individual productions can be incorporated into marketing campaigns, as well as the overall sponsorship of the theatre company.
Royal Insurance, the RSC's long-time insurer and now Royal Sun Alliance, became the theatre company's first sponsor in 1984.
When the insurer decided it would no longer be the RSC's principal sponsor, drinks manufacturer and pub owner Allied Domecq stepped in.
"When Allied Domecq came in they were trying to get some reflected glory from the RSC," said Fleming.

"They wanted to increase awareness of Allied-Domecq's image among the City of London," noted Rowley. Indeed, research has shown that its image did improve over time after it began sponsoring the RSC, he said.
"Allied Domecq," said Fleming, "is leading the way for us and the arts in general by being the single biggest arts sponsor in England."

Allied Domecq, whose brands include Teacher's whisky, Tia Maria liqueur, Courvoisier cognac and Cockburn port, originally signed a three-year sponsorship deal with the RSC. It recently renewed the deal, this time agreeing to sponsor the RSC over five years for 5.5 million pounds.
"What Allied has tried to do is identify specific theatres or productions (of the RSC) with particular traits or brands," said Rowley.

So Allied's Firkin pub group, for instance, is looking at the RSC's more experimental productions that draw younger theatre goers similar to Firkin's clientele. Firkins this summer will hold theatre pub quizzes to build on that link.
"The Firkin relationship helps us reach young audiences whom we don't normally reach," said Rowley. "It builds a more positive response to theatre than young people might hold."
Other ways that Allied Domecq markets its relationship with the RSC is by sponsoring overseas tours of the company, such as Beefeaters gin tour of the RSC in Japan.
The RSC also encourages sponsors to be more pro-active in supporting their deals. "It means promotions, it means advertising," said Fleming.
Citroen cars, part of France's PSA Peugeot Citroen, recently used its sponsorship of an RSC production of "Hamlet" to market its cars to playgoers via a lobby display for a chance to win a Citroen.
The RSC, however, makes it clear that the sponsorship deals in no way cheapen its own image.
"Sponsors are not going to want their logo on Hamlet's costume," said Rowley.
Indeed, sponsors ally themselves with the company because it offers a link to an educated, affluent audience.
"There's a far greater association between the theatre-goer and the sponsor than the beer-swilling, hamburger-eating football-goer," said Fleming.
